articles.title: Public health round-up.
articles.content:
One Health action plan extended

The quadripartite collaboration on One Health, comprising the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, United Nations Environment Programme, World Health Organization and the World Organisation for Animal Health, has extended the implementation of the One Health Joint plan of action from its original 2022–2026 period to 2029. This extension provides countries with greater predictability to plan, implement and scale national One Health priorities, while enabling continued alignment among governments, partners and stakeholders. The plan will remain the shared framework for coordinated, multisectoral action to prevent, detect and respond to health risks at the human, animal, plant and ecosystem interface.

Climate, migration and health agenda

The World Health Organization (WHO) has launched a new global research agenda and action plan to address the health impacts of climate-related migration and displacement, bringing together more than 300 participants from over 75 countries. The initiative aims to strengthen the evidence base on how climate change affects population mobility, health outcomes and access to care.

As climate change increasingly contributes to migration and displacement, significant evidence gaps remain on how climate-related mobility affects health, well-being and access to health care, particularly for vulnerable populations.

“Closing research gaps is a matter of equity. To achieve universal health coverage, strengthen climate resilience and advance health equity, migrant and displaced populations must not be an afterthought, they must be part of the solution from the beginning,” said Santino Severoni, head of WHO’s special initiative on health and migration

Developed through WHO’s Global research prioritization exercise, the agenda identifies priority areas including universal health coverage, emergency preparedness, migration-sensitive data systems, mental health and the long-term health impacts of climate-related mobility.

By strengthening partnerships and supporting evidence-based decision-making, the roadmap aims to advance more resilient, climate-responsive and migrant-inclusive health systems worldwide.

https://bit.ly/4gpkIps

Community evidence for Bundibugyo virus disease

The World Health Organization (WHO) has received a 3 million United States dollars grant from Wellcome to strengthen the use of community-generated evidence in the response to the ongoing Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak. The funding will support the integration of social and behavioural insights alongside epidemiological, clinical and laboratory data, helping authorities make faster and more effective public health decisions.

Since the outbreak was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in May 2026, WHO and partners have been conducting rapid community assessments in affected areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. These assessments capture how people perceive risk, access health care, respond to public health measures and experience the wider impacts of the outbreak.

Findings are already informing operational improvements, including stronger community surveillance, better access to health hotlines, expanded psychosocial support for health workers and clearer communication of laboratory results. The evidence has also identified ways to boost confidence in treatment services by reducing ambulance delays and improving patient reception capacities.

"Every outbreak is shaped not only by the pathogen, but also by how people understand risk, access care and respond to public health measures,” said Chikwe Ihekweazu, executive director of WHO’s health emergencies programme. “This investment is about making social analytics part of how outbreak intelligence works in practice. By integrating community-generated evidence throughout the response, we can build a more complete picture of the outbreak and make faster, more effective decisions that ultimately save lives."

As the Bundibugyo virus disease response continues, WHO and its partners are working to ensure that community-generated evidence becomes a routine component of outbreak intelligence, helping decision-makers respond more quickly, build trust and improve the effectiveness of public health interventions during this outbreak and future health emergencies.

https://bit.ly/4wu3exV

Research4Life at 25

On July 21, WHO marked the 25th anniversary of Research4Life, a public-private partnership that provides researchers, educators, health professionals and policy-makers in low- and middle-income countries with free or low-cost access to scientific literature.

Launched by WHO in 2001 as a pilot initiative with six publishing partners, Research4Life has grown into one of the world's largest partnerships focused on equitable access to scientific publications. Today, it brings together more than 185 publishers and partner organizations, providing over 12 000 institutions in more than 120 countries with access to more than 250 000 journals, books and databases.

"What began as an effort to close the knowledge gap in health has grown into a global movement for research equity," said Sylvie Briand, WHO chief scientist. "For 25 years, Research4Life has helped ensure that researchers, educators, health professionals and policy-makers everywhere can access the evidence they need to improve lives and advance sustainable development."

In addition to improving access to scientific publications, Research4Life now supports researcher training, publishing skills and international collaboration. Through its 2030 strategy, the partnership aims to address persistent barriers to knowledge sharing, including publication costs that continue to limit the ability of many researchers to disseminate their work.

https://bit.ly/4xoEWa9

Greener pharmaceuticals

WHO has launched the first global framework to help medicines regulators support the transition to lower-carbon pharmaceutical systems while maintaining standards of quality, safety, efficacy and equitable access.

The framework, Towards a greener pharmaceuticals' regulatory highway, outlines how regulators can use existing tools, including standards, scientific guidance, reliance mechanisms, digitalization and innovative regulatory pathways, to encourage the adoption of more sustainable technologies across the pharmaceutical lifecycle.

Health systems are estimated to account for around 5% of global greenhouse gas emissions, with pharmaceutical products contributing through manufacturing, packaging, transport, use and disposal. The new framework focuses on enabling wider uptake of existing decarbonization solutions while avoiding unnecessary regulatory burden, delays or barriers to access.

Priority actions include strengthening climate literacy among regulators, improving alignment on emissions measurement and reporting, expanding digital regulatory services, streamlining sustainability-related post-approval changes and promoting greater collaboration between regulatory authorities.

“As regulators, we are not passive actors in this system; we are architects of it,” said Delese Mimi Darko, director general of the African Medicines Agency. “By embedding sustainability into our regulatory frameworks, we can support innovation, strengthen local manufacturing and build more resilient health systems that ensure patients continue to have access to quality safe and efficacious medical products."

The framework is designed to support a just and inclusive transition, ensuring that sustainability efforts do not compromise access to medicines, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

https://bit.ly/4wxdQfo

New leishmaniasis treatment guidelines

WHO has issued updated treatment guidelines for visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar, and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, recommending shorter, safer and more effective treatment regimens for patients in eastern Africa and South-East Asia.

Leishmaniasis is one of the world's deadliest parasitic diseases, causing an estimated 50 000 to 90 000 cases annually. If left untreated, visceral leishmaniasis can be fatal, while post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, a skin condition that may develop after treatment, can contribute to ongoing transmission and is often associated with stigma and social isolation.

“For too long, patients suffering from leishmaniasis have endured treatments nearly as punishing as the disease itself, especially in Africa. These new WHO guidelines mark a turning point,” said Daniel Ngamije Madandi, WHO director of malaria and neglected tropical diseases. “By recommending safer, shorter and more patient-friendly regimens, we are not just improving care; we are accelerating our fight to eliminate this devastating disease and offering renewed hope to communities across Africa and Asia.”

For the first time, WHO recommends sodium stibogluconate-free treatment options for eligible patients. New regimens include oral miltefosine combined with paromomycin for visceral leishmaniasis and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis in eastern Africa, and shorter combination therapies using liposomal amphotericin B and miltefosine for post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis in South-East Asia.

https://bit.ly/4xoHXat

Cover photo

Naomi Kembi and her daughter sit together outside their home in Kilifi County, Kenya. Naomi survived stage 3 cervical cancer and she now advocates for HPV vaccination. In November 2025, Kenya transitioned from a two-dose to a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule, following WHO SAGE recommendations.

Looking ahead

1–30 September. World sexual and reproductive health month 2026. Virtual events. https://bit.ly/4coW6vA

16–18 September. Third meeting of the Global Initiative on AI for Health. https://bit.ly/4x06sKD

articles.title: Molecular Public Health for Infectious Disease Prevention and Control
articles.authors: Kimura H, Kimura R, Mizukoshi F, Shikichi A, Tsukagoshi H, Tomita H, Ryo A.
articles.content:
1. Introduction

Infectious disease microbiology developed around linking specific microorganisms to disease and around microscopy, staining, culture, biochemical identification, serology, and experimental criteria for microbial causation [1,2,3]. These approaches established the foundations of clinical microbiology and infectious disease epidemiology, but they were constrained by culture requirements, variable growth characteristics, limited discriminatory power, and difficulty identifying fastidious or phenotypically unidentifiable organisms [2,3,4]. Improvements in phenotypic identification, including matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization–time of flight mass spectrometry, shortened organism identification after culture, while multiplex assays broadened the number of pathogens detectable in a single clinical episode [5,6]. Collectively, microbiological diagnosis began to shift from descriptive observation of microbial phenotype toward rapid extraction of biologically specific information from clinical specimens [3,5,6].

The intellectual basis for the next transition was provided by twentieth-century molecular biology. The demonstration that deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) carries heritable biological information and elucidation of its double-helical structure established a molecular framework for understanding microbial inheritance, mutation, and evolution [7,8]. Chain-termination sequencing made nucleotide sequence experimentally accessible, allowing microbial variation to be described at the level of individual bases rather than only by morphology, antigenicity, or biochemical behavior [9]. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) transformed infectious disease diagnostics by enabling selective amplification of microbial nucleic acids directly from specimens and reducing dependence on cultivation [10,11]. Real-time PCR added rapid quantification and kinetic monitoring, making temporal changes in nucleic-acid concentration measurable parameters for diagnosis and surveillance [12]. These advances established a central premise of contemporary molecular microbiology: microbial identity, abundance, variation, and evolution can be inferred directly from molecular information [9,10,11,12].

High-throughput sequencing produced a further qualitative change because microbiological investigation was no longer limited to predefined targets or short genetic regions. Whole-genome sequencing can simultaneously provide information on pathogen identity, lineage, mutations, virulence-associated determinants, antimicrobial resistance, and genetic relatedness, thereby linking laboratory characterization directly to epidemiological investigation [13,14]. During the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) pandemic, analytical systems such as Nextstrain, Pangolin, and UShER demonstrated that pathogen genomes could be classified, phylogenetically placed, and visualized at a scale compatible with near-real-time surveillance [15,16,17]. Large-scale genomic analyses further showed that sequence data could reconstruct repeated introductions, lineage replacement, and transmission dynamics at population level [18]. In healthcare settings, rapid sequencing integrated with epidemiological metadata has helped distinguish probable nosocomial transmission from unrelated introductions and has informed infection prevention and control decisions [19,20]. Thus, the unit of microbiological interpretation expanded from the individual organism and patient to transmission networks and pathogen populations [14,18,19,20].

This expansion made bioinformatics inseparable from modern public health microbiology because sequence generation alone does not produce epidemiological meaning. Raw molecular data must be transformed through quality control, read processing, mapping or assembly, consensus generation, variant calling, lineage assignment, phylogenetic reconstruction, functional annotation, and linkage with temporal, geographic, clinical, and exposure metadata [14,21,22]. These analytical steps determine whether a genomic difference represents technical noise, within-host variation, a new lineage, a transmission cluster, or a resistance-associated mutation [14,21,22]. Bioinformatics therefore functions not merely as computational support but as the interpretive engine that converts molecular measurements into structured evidence for epidemiological inference and public health action [14,21,22,23]. Reproducibility, version control, standardized reference datasets, and transparent uncertainty reporting become increasingly important as surveillance becomes automated, distributed, and high volume [21,22,24,25,26,27].

Moreover, the molecular field has simultaneously expanded beyond isolate-based genomics. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing can detect microbial nucleic acids without requiring a pathogen-specific hypothesis and therefore provides a route to identifying unexpected, difficult-to-culture, or previously unrecognized infectious agents [28,29,30,31]. It can also characterize viromes, bacteriomes, resistomes, and mixed microbial communities, although interpretation depends strongly on contamination control, database quality, taxonomic classification, and meaningful reporting thresholds [28,29,30,31]. Wastewater sequencing extends molecular observation from the patient to the community and can reveal transmission patterns or viral lineages incompletely represented by clinical testing [32,33,34]. Long-read sequencing further increases bacterial genomic resolution by resolving structural variation, plasmids, and mobile resistance elements that may be incompletely reconstructed by short-read sequencing [35]. Molecular surveillance can therefore observe pathogens across individuals, populations, microbial communities, and environmental reservoirs rather than within the boundaries of conventional clinical testing alone [28,29,30,31,32,33,34,35].

Thus, these technological changes have also altered the organization of public health microbiology. Contemporary systems require integration of laboratory science, bioinformatics, epidemiology, data engineering, governance, and communication. For public health practice, end-to-end turnaround from specimen collection to an interpretable report is an operationally critical performance measure, not sequencing speed in isolation [19,20,21,23]. The World Health Organization (WHO) Global Genomic Surveillance Strategy for Pathogens with Pandemic and Epidemic Potential 2022–2032 explicitly frames genomic surveillance as part of an end-to-end system that includes sampling, diagnostics, analysis, data sharing, and connectivity among disease-control programs [36]. WHO guidance for wastewater and environmental surveillance similarly emphasizes integration with other surveillance streams and implementation where results can support meaningful public health decisions [37]. These developments parallel the movement from public health genomics toward precision public health, in which increasingly granular biological and population data are used to improve the timing and targeting of prevention strategies [38,39].

Against this historical and technological background, an important conceptual gap remains. Molecular diagnostics, molecular epidemiology, genomic epidemiology, pathogen genomics for public health, and precision public health are established constructs, yet the literature often treats clinical genomics, wastewater and environmental surveillance, One Health, antimicrobial resistance, metagenomics, and computational prediction as partly separate domains [14,32,36,37,38,39,40]. We therefore define molecular public health as the integrated application of molecular microbiology, genomics, bioinformatics, epidemiology, and population surveillance to convert molecular information on pathogens and their ecological contexts into population-level risk assessment, decision-making, intervention, and evaluation. Molecular epidemiology is an essential component of this framework rather than a competing concept: it establishes molecular distributions and relationships, whereas molecular public health explicitly extends those inferences through an end-to-end operational pathway in which a molecular result becomes public health information only when it changes, or is capable of changing, what is done [14,19,20,36]. The framework also differs from precision public health in emphasis: precision public health uses increasingly granular biological and population data to improve the timing and targeting of prevention across health domains, whereas molecular public health centers specifically on molecular evidence concerning infectious agents, hosts, and reservoirs and its translation into infectious-disease prevention and control [38,39]. Accordingly, the principal evaluative criteria are actionability, timeliness, interpretability, reproducibility, equity, and measurable contribution to prevention and control rather than technological sophistication alone. The following sections therefore examine not only what each molecular technology can measure, but also how molecular evidence can be integrated into an operational decision cycle.

2. Review Scope and Literature Selection

This article was designed as a state-of-the-art narrative review rather than a formal systematic review. Literature selection was purposive and iterative, prioritizing publications from 2021 to 2026 while retaining foundational studies needed to explain the historical and analytical development of molecular public health. Targeted PubMed/MEDLINE searches and checks of authoritative public-health guidance were conducted for literature available through 14 September 2026, with particular attention to implementation, validation, equity, economic evaluation, wastewater normalization, and artificial intelligence. The aim was to achieve transparent, current coverage of the major conceptual and operational domains rather than exhaustive systematic enumeration. Search concepts were combined iteratively around molecular diagnostics, pathogen genomics, genomic surveillance, bioinformatics, genomic epidemiology, phylodynamics, metagenomics or pathogen-agnostic sequencing, wastewater or environmental surveillance, One Health, antimicrobial resistance genomics, host response or multi-omics, artificial intelligence or machine learning, implementation, public-health action, and infectious-disease control. Authoritative guidance from the World Health Organization and other public-health bodies was prioritized for questions of implementation, standardization, governance, and surveillance integration [36,37,41]. Priority was given to peer-reviewed primary studies, systematic or scoping reviews, implementation evaluations, and guidance documents that directly informed population surveillance, outbreak investigation, prevention, control, governance, or implementation. Studies focused solely on molecular mechanism or individual-patient diagnosis without a clear population or public-health implication were generally not prioritized. Because selection was purposive and iterative rather than prospectively systematic, no PRISMA record count or meta-analysis is presented; this limitation is stated explicitly so that readers can judge coverage and potential selection bias.

3. Conceptual Framework from Molecular Epidemiology to Molecular Public Health

For organizing the decision pathway, we use the established analytics terminology of descriptive, predictive, and prescriptive analysis, with an explicit analytical/interpretive stage inserted to reflect the requirements of infectious-disease surveillance [42]. This sequence is used as a heuristic for public-health translation rather than proposed as a new general analytics taxonomy. The descriptive stage identifies which pathogen, lineage, mutation, resistance determinant, or molecular signal is present; the analytical stage determines how those signals are related in time, place, host, and population; the predictive stage estimates what is likely to happen next; and the prescriptive stage links the resulting risk estimate to a feasible intervention. Molecular and genomic epidemiology contribute principally to the descriptive and analytical stages and increasingly to prediction. Molecular public health adds an explicit operational requirement that these stages be connected to a decision owner, intervention window, intervention, and post-intervention evaluation. It also broadens the surveillance architecture by integrating clinical, genomic, wastewater, food, animal, vector, and environmental signals where appropriate [32,33,34,36,37]. Table 1 summarizes the relationship between molecular public health and adjacent constructs. The progression from molecular detection to population-level public health action is summarized in Figure 1.

4. Bioinformatics and Data Integration: The Interpretive Engine of Molecular Public Health

Because the molecular public health framework depends on interpretation rather than sequence generation alone, bioinformatics occupies a central position between the laboratory and the public health decision [14,21,22,23]. Routine genomic workflows typically include raw-read quality assessment, adapter and low-quality trimming, contamination screening, reference mapping or de novo assembly, consensus generation, variant calling, lineage or sequence-type assignment, phylogenetic placement, and functional annotation [14,22,44]. Reproducible workflow managers and analysis environments such as Snakemake, Nextflow, and Galaxy allow complex pipelines to be versioned, automated, and transferred between laboratories, thereby reducing analytical heterogeneity [24,25,26]. For public health use, these computational outputs must be integrated with curated metadata and rendered as interpretable products such as cluster reports, lineage-frequency summaries, resistance alerts, phylogenetic visualizations, or dashboards [15,16,17,21,23]. Accreditation, validated pipelines, external quality assessment, version-controlled reference datasets, and explicit reporting of uncertainty are therefore essential components of implementation rather than optional technical refinements [27,45]. Recent implementation frameworks increasingly treat end-to-end genomic surveillance—including informatics and interpretation—as a public health service that should be evaluated for timeliness, reproducibility, and impact on control decisions [43,45,46]. The end-to-end pathway from sampling and laboratory outputs through bioinformatic interpretation to public health action is illustrated in Figure 2.

The principal bioinformatic functions required to convert molecular data into interpretable public health intelligence are summarized in Table 2.

5. Molecular Detection and Quantification Technologies

Reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) is widely used for predefined-target molecular surveillance because it is rapid, sensitive, scalable, and well standardized [3,12,36,37]. Digital PCR provides absolute quantification without reliance on a standard curve and can improve precision for low-copy targets or inhibitor-rich matrices [51]. Multiplex molecular panels increase syndromic breadth but remain constrained by assay design [6], whereas CRISPR-based detection offers rapid, potentially field-deployable testing, although sample processing, multiplexing, quantitative workflows, and end-to-end standardization remain implementation challenges [52,53,54]. These approaches do not have equivalent implementation maturity. For the purposes of this review, established denotes routine public-health use in multiple defined settings; context-dependent denotes operational use with substantial pathogen-, infrastructure-, or jurisdiction-specific constraints; and emerging denotes applications for which routine population-level implementation or demonstrated decision impact remains limited. These descriptors refer to implementation maturity rather than analytical validity and should not be interpreted as a universal ranking. The principal molecular technologies used across the molecular public health continuum are summarized in Table 3.

Indicative implementation maturity: established for targeted PCR/multiplex PCR and short-read WGS in defined surveillance or outbreak applications; established but context-dependent for dPCR and amplicon sequencing; context-dependent and expanding for long-read/hybrid sequencing; and generally emerging or highly context-dependent for pathogen-agnostic metagenomics and CRISPR-based integrated surveillance [14,43,53,54,58,60].

6. Next-Generation Sequencing and Pathogen Genomic Surveillance

Whole-genome sequencing provides high-resolution information on pathogen variation and has become a core platform for lineage surveillance, outbreak investigation, source attribution, and resistance characterization [13,14]. Short-read sequencing remains advantageous for high accuracy and throughput, whereas long-read sequencing can resolve structural variation, complete genomes, plasmids, and other mobile elements that are difficult to reconstruct from short reads alone [35]. Portable sequencing demonstrated during Ebola and subsequent outbreaks that genomic surveillance can be moved closer to the field and can provide information during an ongoing public health emergency [56]. National and regional programs now increasingly emphasize standardized sampling, automated bioinformatics, data integration, and rapid interpretation rather than sequencing capacity in isolation [27,36,43,45,46].

7. Genomic Epidemiology and Phylodynamics

Genomic epidemiology integrates pathogen sequence data with temporal, geographic, and host information to infer introductions, clusters, transmission patterns, and pathogen movement [14,18]. SARS-CoV-2 studies demonstrated that dense genomic sampling can reconstruct epidemic establishment and lineage dynamics at national scale, while growth-rate and phylodynamic analyses can identify variants with altered transmission characteristics [18,47,48,49]. Similar approaches have been used to characterize the international emergence and microevolution of mpox virus and other rapidly spreading pathogens [50]. Nevertheless, genomic similarity is not proof of direct transmission, and public health interpretation must explicitly account for incomplete sampling, evolutionary rate, epidemiological plausibility, and uncertainty [14,19,20].

8. Metagenomics and Pathogen-Agnostic Surveillance

Metagenomic sequencing extends molecular surveillance beyond predefined targets and is therefore particularly relevant to difficult-to-diagnose infections and preparedness for emerging or re-emerging pathogens [28,29,30,31,57,58]. Public health pathogen-agnostic sequencing programs have highlighted both its potential and its operational constraints, including host-background nucleic acid, contamination, sequencing depth, reference-database bias, computational demand, and difficulties assigning clinical or epidemiological significance to low-abundance findings [30,57,58]. Environmental applications are also expanding, with metagenomic sequencing detecting respiratory and enteric viral signals in air collected from congregate settings [59]. The central implementation requirement is a validated interpretive pathway that distinguishes unusual but genuine signals from analytical noise and defines when a finding should be escalated for confirmatory testing or epidemiological investigation [30,31,57,58].

9. Wastewater and Environmental Surveillance

Wastewater and environmental surveillance (WES) provides population-level molecular information independent of individual healthcare-seeking behavior and therefore complements case-based surveillance [32,33,34,37,61]. During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, wastewater sequencing detected cryptic SARS-CoV-2 lineages and provided information on variant circulation that was not fully captured by clinical sequencing [32,33]. The approach is now being generalized to other respiratory and enteric pathogens and to antimicrobial resistance, but quantitative comparison is affected by shedding biology, catchment structure, dilution and inflow, recovery efficiency, sampling design, and the denominator used to represent the contributing population [34,37,61,62]. Normalization strategies include flow- or mass-load normalization, fecal-strength or fecal-indicator markers, process/recovery controls, and estimated catchment population; these choices can materially alter between-site comparisons, and no single normalization method is universally optimal [61,62]. Real-world reviews indicate that WES can trigger testing, communication, outbreak investigation, or other interventions, but detection-to-action pathways remain heterogeneous and are often not prospectively defined [63]. Future systems therefore require explicit action thresholds, transparent reporting of normalization assumptions and uncertainty, and integration of wastewater signals with clinical, genomic, and epidemiological surveillance [37,61,62,63].

10. One Health Molecular Surveillance

The ability to compare molecular information across human, animal, food, and environmental sources makes One Health a natural extension of molecular public health [36,40]. Genomic surveillance can help identify zoonotic spillover, distinguish sustained human transmission from repeated animal-to-human introductions, and connect foodborne cases with agricultural or environmental sources [14,40,64]. Whole-genome sequencing has already transformed foodborne disease surveillance by improving discrimination among closely related isolates and strengthening outbreak detection and source attribution [64]. The major remaining challenge is interoperability because different sectors frequently use incompatible metadata standards, sampling strategies, legal frameworks, and reporting systems [36,40]. The integration of molecular surveillance across human, animal, food, environmental, and vector domains is illustrated in Figure 3.

11. Molecular Public Health Approaches to Antimicrobial Resistance

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is particularly suited to a molecular public health framework because resistance can spread through clonal expansion, mutation, horizontal gene transfer, mobile genetic elements, and movement across healthcare, community, food, animal, and environmental reservoirs [35,40,65]. Genomic analysis can identify resistance determinants and high-risk clones, while long-read sequencing can resolve plasmid context and help distinguish clonal transmission from dissemination of mobile resistance elements [35,40]. However, genotype and phenotype are not interchangeable. The presence of a resistance determinant may not produce the expected phenotypic resistance because expression, regulatory effects, gene context, epistasis, breakpoint definitions, and incomplete reference databases can alter the observed phenotype; conversely, resistance may arise through mechanisms not represented in current reference sets [66]. Machine-learning methods increasingly use genome content and sequence variation to predict antimicrobial susceptibility or resistance, but performance depends on representative phenotype-linked training data, organism- and drug-specific validation, and external evaluation [66]. Genomic prediction should therefore complement rather than automatically replace phenotypic antimicrobial-susceptibility testing when individual treatment decisions are involved. Public health value is achieved when validated molecular findings influence stewardship, empirical-treatment policy, outbreak control, environmental investigation, or prioritization of emerging resistance threats [40,65,66].

12. Beyond Genomics: Multi-Omics and Host-Response Surveillance

Pathogen genomes do not capture the full biology of infection, and transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and serological approaches can provide complementary information on host response, severity, immune status, and disease heterogeneity [67,68]. COVID-19 multi-omic studies, for example, identified coordinated immunologic and metabolic states associated with disease severity and transitions between clinical states [67,68]. These findings illustrate biological and risk-stratification potential, but most remain discovery- or research-stage observations rather than validated population-level action triggers [67,68]. For public-health implementation, high-dimensional signatures must be reduced to robust assays or reproducible computational outputs, prospectively validated in the intended population, generated within a relevant intervention window, and linked to a defined decision. Multi-omics should therefore be regarded as an emerging augmentation to pathogen-centered molecular surveillance rather than an operational equivalent of routine PCR or established genomic surveillance. Its most plausible near-term role is targeted host-risk stratification or mechanistic enrichment of surveillance in settings where the added information changes prioritization, resource allocation, or evaluation of interventions.

13. Artificial Intelligence and Computational Public Health

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning can support selected molecular public-health tasks, including AMR prediction, anomaly detection, forecasting, and integration of heterogeneous surveillance streams [66,69,70]. A concrete molecular-data application is genome-based AMR prediction, in which machine-learning models infer susceptibility from genome content or sequence variation; performance is strongly dependent on organism, antimicrobial, training-data composition, and external validation [66]. At the broader surveillance level, recent reviews describe AI-enabled early-warning systems that integrate epidemiological, environmental, web, wastewater, and sometimes genomic data, while also showing that much of the published evidence remains retrospective, proof-of-concept, or locally validated rather than prospectively embedded in routine public-health decision pathways [69,70]. This implementation gap is itself important. A high-performing model should not be considered actionable until it has been externally validated in independent populations, prospectively evaluated in the intended workflow, calibrated for the decision threshold, assessed for bias and interpretability, and monitored for data or concept drift [69,70]. Operational evaluation should test whether the model improves time to detection, prioritization, resource allocation, or intervention outcomes compared with existing surveillance. AI is therefore best regarded as an analytical accelerator within the molecular public-health architecture, with accountability remaining with the public-health system using the model.

14. Translating Molecular Data into Infectious Disease Control

The defining feature of molecular public health is translation from molecular signal to public health action [14,36]. Genomic and other molecular data can support outbreak detection, transmission-chain investigation, targeted screening, cohorting, ward-level infection prevention and control (IPC), vaccination strategies, food traceback, source remediation, and antimicrobial stewardship when the analytical result is linked to an operational decision [19,20,36,40,63,65]. We define actionability as the condition in which molecular information has sufficient analytical validity, epidemiological interpretability, timeliness, and linkage to a feasible intervention to change a public-health decision within the relevant action window. This definition deliberately does not impose a universal numerical cutoff: an acceptable turnaround time, genomic distance, wastewater increase, or predictive probability depends on pathogen biology, sampling density, surveillance purpose, intervention availability, and jurisdiction. Action thresholds should therefore be prospectively specified and locally validated rather than retrospectively inferred after an outbreak [36,37,63].

Operationalizing Actionability

Actionability can nevertheless be measured through a common set of dimensions. Candidate metrics include sample-to-decision time relative to the intervention window; the proportion of molecular reports that confirm, modify, escalate, or de-escalate a public-health action; concordance with epidemiological or phenotypic evidence; discrimination and calibration when predictive models are used; incremental yield over conventional surveillance; and post-intervention changes in transmission, shedding, cases, resistance, or response time [19,20,36,43,45,63]. These metrics should be selected before implementation and interpreted against a pre-specified baseline or counterfactual whenever feasible. Table 5 provides a practical measurement framework.

15. Challenges: Standardization, Ethics, Equity, and Governance

Technical barriers include sampling bias, insufficient denominators, incomplete metadata, contamination, pipeline heterogeneity, slow turnaround, and inconsistent reporting standards [27,36,43,45,46]. Implementation also depends on total resource requirements rather than sequencing reagent cost alone: platform acquisition and maintenance, batching and throughput, quality systems, data storage, bioinformatics, workforce, confirmatory testing, and reporting infrastructure all contribute to sustainability [45,60,71]. Comparative economic evidence remains incomplete. A 2023 systematic review found that the economic evidence supporting broad front-line WGS implementation was limited and heterogeneous, reinforcing the need to evaluate costs together with decision impact rather than assuming that greater molecular resolution is automatically cost-effective [71]. Metagenomic surveillance can provide pathogen-agnostic breadth, but its computational and financial burden is particularly relevant in resource-scarce settings, where targeted molecular assays or regionalized sequencing may answer the public-health question more efficiently [72].

Technical success also does not guarantee public-health impact. In the multicentre COG-UK HOCI prospective study, rapid SARS-CoV-2 sequencing changed IPC practice in a subset of hospital-onset cases but did not produce a statistically significant reduction in nosocomial infection incidence overall; the practical effect was greater when reports were returned within five days, whereas high case volume and constrained response capacity limited implementation [20]. Similarly, wastewater studies show that pathogen detection can lead to testing, communication, outbreak investigation, or other actions, but the link between detection and intervention remains inconsistent across settings [63]. These mixed outcomes illustrate why turnaround, decision ownership, response capacity, and outcome evaluation must be treated as part of the molecular system rather than as external implementation details.

Equity requires a resource-adaptive rather than technology-maximal approach. The preferred method should be the least complex platform that can answer the defined public-health question reliably and within the action window. Practical adaptations include sentinel rather than exhaustive sampling, targeted PCR or amplicon approaches when adequate, regional sequencing hubs, shared bioinformatics, transferable validated workflows, minimum interoperable metadata sets, workforce development, and integration with existing surveillance programs [36,72,73,74]. Unequal sequencing intensity also creates inferential bias: regions with limited capacity contribute fewer genomes and metadata, potentially distorting apparent lineage distributions, transmission routes, and AMR patterns [73,74,75]. Equity and representativeness should therefore be treated as measurable properties of surveillance performance, not only as downstream ethical considerations.

The major implementation challenges and corresponding practical responses are summarized in Table 6.

16. Future Perspectives Toward Closed-Loop Predictive Molecular Public Health

The next stage of molecular public health will move beyond retrospective characterization toward closed-loop systems in which surveillance generates molecular signals, bioinformatics converts those signals into structured risk information, predictive models estimate likely trajectories, decision-makers intervene, and subsequent surveillance measures the effect of intervention [14,36,39]. The SARS-CoV-2 experience demonstrated both the feasibility of global genomic surveillance and the consequences of unequal sequencing intensity, incomplete metadata, and variable integration with decision-making [18,75]. Future systems may combine pathogen-agnostic surveillance, real-time sequencing, wastewater and environmental monitoring, long-read genomics, host-response data, and multimodal AI within interoperable architectures, but such components should be adopted when they add validated decision value rather than simply increase technological complexity [31,35,37,58,69,70]. Progress should therefore be measured by earlier detection, more reliable interpretation, faster or better-targeted decisions, equitable coverage, and demonstrable intervention impact. As an illustrative operational workflow, consider a hospital in which two temporally linked hospital-onset infections trigger rapid sequencing under a pre-specified IPC protocol. Sequence and metadata integration first determines whether the cases are compatible with a shared transmission cluster; the report is then returned within the locally defined IPC action window and linked to a decision rule for targeted screening, cohorting, environmental investigation, or reinforcement of precautions. Subsequent molecular and epidemiological surveillance measures new cluster-associated cases over a defined follow-up period. If transmission does not decline, the decision rule or intervention is revised. The relevant performance measures are therefore not only sequence quality or phylogenetic resolution but also time to report, proportion of reports changing IPC, cluster-associated incidence, and the post-intervention trajectory [19,20,43,45]. The exact time and genomic thresholds are pathogen- and setting-specific; the closed-loop principle is the prospective linkage of signal, decision, intervention, and feedback. This closed-loop decision architecture is illustrated in Figure 4.

17. Conclusions

Molecular public health is best understood as an operational architecture for converting molecular evidence into population-level prevention and control, not as a replacement for molecular or genomic epidemiology. Across the evidence reviewed, targeted molecular detection, short-read pathogen genomics, standardized bioinformatics, and genomics-supported outbreak investigation already have established roles in defined public-health settings, whereas pathogen-agnostic metagenomics, multi-omics, and AI-enabled decision support have more heterogeneous implementation maturity. Wastewater, long-read, and One Health approaches occupy context-dependent positions: their technical value is increasingly demonstrated, but action thresholds, standardization, infrastructure requirements, and integration with conventional surveillance remain variable [35,36,37,43,60,63]. The principal limitations are therefore not only analytical. Sampling bias, turnaround, metadata quality, interoperability, workforce and infrastructure, governance, cost, and unequal global representation determine whether a molecular signal can actually change a decision [20,45,71,72,73,74]. Key knowledge gaps include prospectively validated action thresholds, comparative implementation and economic evaluations, external and prospective validation of predictive models, and evidence that molecularly informed interventions improve outcomes. The practical implication is that future progress should be judged by validated decision impact, timeliness, equity, and measurable improvement in prevention and control rather than by the volume or technological sophistication of molecular data generated.

articles.title: Assessing the public health informatics workforce in Texas local health departments
articles.authors: Leos R, Hammarberg R, Valerio-Shewmaker M, Baker K.
articles.content:
Introduction

Health departments have faced many challenges in the integration and management of informatics within their organizations. While state health departments have contributed their expertise locally, local health department (LHD) staff must be able to carry out a wide range of informatics activities without the assistance of the state (1). A capacity and needs assessment survey conducted in 2015 described LHDs' top informatics activities as the extraction of data from information systems (69.5%) and the use and interpretation of quantitative (66.4%) and qualitative (55.1%) data while using geographic information systems (45.0%) or other analytical software (39.7%) (1). Unfortunately, research has shown that most public health professionals may not possess the necessary skills to use information effectively or even be aware of the importance of informatics (2). One study assessing awareness about public health trends found that only a little over half (55.6%) of LHD employees had any awareness that “leveraging electronic health information” was a public health trend (2). Furthermore, 49 in-depth key informant interviews with LHD professionals revealed that LHDs had too few informatics staff and limited informatics training (3). Other related concerns included “dated data, aging infrastructure, lack of training capacity, and insufficient time to complete tasks” (3).

These informatics-related challenges are also reflected in the Texas workforce. With a decentralized public health structure (local governments determine public health funding and services), Texas has over 170 local public health organizations (4, 5). Over 180 counties do not have an LHD and rely on the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) for all public health services (6). According to the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) Profile of State and Territorial Public Health, Texas DSHS had 36 health informatics specialist full-time equivalent positions (filled and vacant) in 2022, representing only 1% of the workforce (7). The Texas Tribune's database of compensation for Texas state employees also showed that 1% of DSHS employees were in a public health informatics specialist position as of July 2026 (8). While these percentages are not specific to local organizations or LHDs, past research has found that most LHDs lack a dedicated informatics team. According to NACCHO's most recent Public Health Informatics Profile, only 14% of LHDs reported having a dedicated informatics team or department in 2024, and those with a dedicated team were typically epidemiologists and IT staff (9). A 2025 study analyzing the most recent Public Health Workforce Interests and Needs Survey (PH WINS) data also found that public health informatics (PHI) specialists accounted for 0.5% of large LHDs (members of the Big Cities Health Coalition) and 0.3% of other LHDs (10). To date, no formal comprehensive needs assessment specific to the public health informatics workforce in Texas LHDs has been conducted.

Health informatics can be defined as “the science of how we collect, analyze, and use health information to improve health and healthcare” (11). It is a discipline that converges and shares methodologies with other fields such as data science and epidemiology (12). As a subfield, public health informatics can be defined as the “systematic application of information, computer science, and technology in areas of public health, including surveillance, prevention, preparedness, and health promotion” to “capture, manage, analyze, disseminate, and use information to improve population-level health outcomes” (13, 14). While many LHDs have tasked epidemiologists and IT staff to assist with informatics work, these traditional positions do not always reflect the specialized skills or distinct responsibilities of public health informatics professionals. Public health informatics professionals focus on “integrating and managing data, building stronger data systems, and improving how information flows across programs and partners” (15). The Applied Public Health Informatics Competency Model further outlines specific skill sets and abilities necessary to carry out public health informatics and address challenges in the field. These skills and abilities relate to eight competency areas: Analysis, Visualization, & Reporting; Communications; Evaluation; Information Systems; Policy; Principles & Strategies; Project Management; and Standards & Interoperability (16). These public health informatics competencies ultimately affect LHDs' ability to address health disparities. Past research examining the effect of public health informatics in addressing disparities found that LHDs with greater use of information systems had “higher levels of engagement in performing activities to address health disparities and health inequities” (17).

With a vision to address the challenges outlined in the literature and expand efforts that would strengthen the public health informatics workforce across Texas, the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston (UTHealth Houston) launched the Gaining Equity in Training for Public Health Informatics and Technology (GET PHIT) initiative and statewide consortium in 2021. The consortium was established with nine partnering Texas universities, which would drive the initiative statewide. With funding from the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy (ASTP) within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the consortium used a comprehensive approach that included bootcamps and internships for university students, professional development courses for workforce professionals, and a workforce needs assessment. The workforce needs assessment was a critical and necessary piece of the initiative that would explore informatics capacities and gaps specific to LHDs and LHD staff in Texas.

Methods

Study design and tools

A mixed-methods approach was utilized to conduct an exploratory study to gain insight into the current public health informatics workforce infrastructure within Texas LHDs (objective 1) and to identify key assets and challenges (objective 2). Literature and assessment tools were reviewed to guide the design of the study's data collection tools. With feedback from GET PHIT consortium members, a participant survey and interview guide were finalized to include participant demographic questions (e.g., age, gender, education) and organizational-level questions adapted from existing self-assessment tools published by the Public Health Informatics Institute and the Kansas Health Institute.

Organizational-level questions aimed to investigate several informatics-related areas, including data collection, data sharing processes, and informatics training. Sample questions included: “Do you currently have procedures for establishing data sharing agreements?”, “Does your organization use audience-specific messaging to communicate the value of public health data in your community?” and “Does your organization support staff members across a broad range of job classifications to participate in informatics training?” Each response option corresponded to a specific maturity level from the Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI) framework, designed to evaluate organizational capabilities and offer guidance for continuous improvement (18). We used two versions of the scale to mirror the Building an Informatics-savvy Health Department: A Self-Assessment Tool and the Kansas Public Health Informatics Self-Assessment Tool (19, 20). Table 1 defines the maturity levels for each version.

Recruitment and data collection

Partnerships between UTHealth Houston, academic institutions, and public health agencies were established before the initiative's official launch. Through these partnerships, purposive sampling was used to identify and recruit LHD staff with insight into their organization's informatics-related work. Beginning in April 2022, recruited LHD staff were sent a link with the study's information letter and survey. Once a participant submitted their survey, they were contacted by the research team to schedule a 1-h virtual interview. Each interview was transcribed via WebEx and reviewed for accuracy. Interviews and data collection concluded in September 2022.

Data analysis

Survey data were reviewed for missingness and uploaded into Stata for analysis. Descriptive statistics summarized demographics, including participants' years of experience, years employed by the organization, gender, race, ethnicity, education, and age. Responses to informatics-related questions were summarized according to three activity categories: data collection, data sharing, and dissemination of information; informatics-related training, support, and resources; and information partnerships to meet community needs. Capability maturity levels were summarized with counts and percentages.

Interview data were analyzed using a multi-step process to identify key themes and patterns. First, a research team member reviewed the recordings and transcripts to ensure the accuracy of the transcripts. After transcripts were finalized, sentences and paragraphs were organized into meaningful segments and assigned labels or “codes” that aligned with the study's objectives. One researcher conducted this initial coding process, while a second researcher reviewed the coded data, specifically looking for potential gaps or discrepancies. Both researchers met several times to discuss differences in interpretation and to finalize codes. After finalizing the codes, emerging patterns or themes were identified and finalized through the same process (one researcher doing the initial round and the second researcher reviewing before meeting together). Themes were presented to the larger team before finalizing to ensure clarity. Finally, a narrative was written to present each theme, supported by examples and direct quotes.

Results

Demographics

After contacting 12 partner LHDs, a total of 11 LHDs responded and helped us identify one staff member to participate on behalf of their department. The 11 staff members who participated included a Data Services Program Manager, Epidemiology and Surveillance Program Manager, Data Analytics Reporting Manager, Informatics Manager, Chief Epidemiologist, Chief of Informatics, Chief of Staff, Assistant Health Administrator, two Directors, and an Assistant Director. Most participants identified as female (n = 10), White (n = 8), and non-Hispanic/Latino (n = 8). Additionally, most were 35+ years of age (n = 9) and held a master's degree (n = 8). The number of years employed by their department ranged from 1–3 years to 10 years+, with the highest percentage being employed for 10 years+ (36.4%). Years of professional public health and informatics experience ranged from no experience to 10 years+. Participants had more years of professional experience in public health (63.6% had a minimum of 7 years) than informatics-specific experience (27.2% had a minimum of 7 years). A complete summary of participant demographics is provided in Table 2. Most participating LHDs (n = 10) were classified as “large” by the Texas Association of City and County Health Officials (TACCHO). Almost half of the participants (n = 5) reported their departments having 100–500 employees, with over half (n = 6) noting that ethnic minorities comprised over 75% of the workforce. While most lacked a dedicated informatics unit, they confirmed having IT support for informatics projects. Table 3 provides a demographic overview of each represented health department.

Survey - maturity levels

When asked about data collection, sharing, and information dissemination processes, over 50% of LHDs selected responses at the systematic level (where department-wide processes are supported by policies) or at the optimized capability maturity level (where department-wide processes are supported by policies and methods to assess needs and improve performance exist). Regarding informatics training, resources, and support, most LHDs (90%) indicated that informatics training was not part of their organizational plan. When asked about supporting staff across various job classifications to participate in informatics training, almost half (45.5%) of LHDs selected responses at the absent or initial capability maturity levels (where there is no capability or only ad hoc efforts). When asked about having appropriate job classifications for informatics positions, over 60% selected responses at either the absent or initial maturity levels. Regarding information partnerships, almost fifty percent indicated they “sometimes” invite community leaders from marginalized groups to participate in public health data system design, content, or use discussions. Additionally, 27% of LHDs selected responses at the optimized maturity level when asked about collaborating effectively with community partners for population health assessment. Results for all survey questions are provided in Table 4.

Interviews

While we aimed to interview the same participants who completed the survey, four participants were no longer available due to retirement, leave, or limited availability. Three of those participants referred us to other staff who could participate on their behalf. Two participants also invited additional team members to be present in the interview. With these changes, we completed a total of 10 interviews (representing 10 of the initial 11 LHDs) with 14 individuals (two interviews had more than one representative). After transcribing and analyzing interview data, we identified three key themes from the qualitative data that highlight the public health informatics infrastructure and the challenges and assets of the workforce in local health departments. While epidemiology teams were often considered central to the informatics infrastructure, other internal programs supported informatics practices (Theme 1). Personnel and resource constraints emerged as significant challenges impacting the ability to conduct informatics work and training (Theme 2). Additionally, established partnerships, both internal and external, proved to be crucial for successful informatics efforts (Theme 3). These themes will be explored further in the following sections.

Theme 1 – multiple units supporting public health informatics

Participants explained how informatics is used in their departments, often referring to “Epidemiology,” “Epidemiologist,” and “Epi staff” for those at the forefront of informatics-related work. Some departments had only one or a few epidemiologists, while others had larger units or sub-teams. An Assistant Director mentioned that their department relies on a single epidemiologist responsible for collecting and organizing data from environmental and clinical sites. While “epidemiology” and “informatics” were often used interchangeably, it was evident that other programs contributed to informatics-related work. One Assistant Director stated, “We are a department that provides direct services…in every division, even though it's segmented, there's some sort of tracking mechanism that monitors the information and productivity through data.” Both clinical and non-clinical programming, such as STD/HIV, tuberculosis, health promotion, and environmental health programs, were identified as actively collecting and sharing data via an electronic medical record (EMR) system or other data reporting systems. Other examples included a workforce development program consisting of a data management team and an information technology team overseeing data access and storage. Participants mostly discussed these programs' role in data sharing, collection, and management, rather than their role in a formal informatics infrastructure.

Theme 2 – resource-related constraints impacting the workforce

As participants discussed workforce gaps or challenges, it was evident that funding and retaining staff were key constraints impacting the ability to pursue informatics-related work efficiently. Although COVID grants made it possible to hire some additional staff to meet pandemic-related demands, participants expressed concerns about funds coming to end and not being able to retain those staff. Past hiring experiences were also shared, and the difficulty in finding professionals with sufficient informatics-related expertise and skills beyond a general master's degree in public health was a challenge. Some participants faced staff turnover and loss of employees to higher-paying opportunities. The shortage in staff was also attributed to underdeveloped training efforts. Participants felt it would be difficult to expand training without the proper staff to lead or oversee it.

Another key constraint was specific to the software and reporting systems used for data collection and sharing. Either the systems were outdated or inoperable. One participant expressed difficulties utilizing a state reporting system and explained, “That's why we had all these cities and municipalities create their systems on the fly for COVID, because the system that the state had cannot handle it?.” Another stressed the difficulties of using internal reporting systems that do not communicate. The participant further explained, “We maintain different systems within our EPI, within our TB or TIs, and then the notification to the state. That's a completely different system, even between the different programs. So, we're talking about six different systems that…don't communicate with each other.?” Some noted they were modernizing software and reporting systems and hiring staff. Others lacked the funding to modernize in the ways they desired.

Theme 3 – partnerships as an asset and strategy for informatics work

All departments faced personnel and resource challenges in informatics work, but they viewed partnerships as a key strategy to mitigate such challenges. Partnerships (formal and informal) with other departments and local government agencies were highlighted by most participating LHDs. One participant stated, “we recently partnered with our department of Human Services Department to collect data on youth mental health, that's been a priority area for us because mental health is incredibly fragile right now for everybody.” Participants shared other examples of partnerships and collaborations, such as working with the IT department on database upgrades, partnering with the Fire Department for COVID data management, and collaborating with the GIS Department to create interactive dashboards. External partnerships were also emphasized, involving stakeholders like universities, non-profits, hospital providers, school districts, and Texas DSHS. One participant expressed, “It wasn't hard to get data from the hospital providers… we have some automatic feeds to get all of their COVID testing and vaccine data.” Another described their department's involvement in a community partners group where multiple stakeholders gather to share data. Some participants mentioned having formal contracts with stakeholders, including one who highlighted their department's agreement with an academic institution for PhD students to assist with data analysis. These collaborations illustrate the entities sharing common goals in public health informatics and the importance of trust and lasting relationships.

Discussion

Our findings highlight public health informatics as an applied practice woven across multiple department programs and divisions, rather than the responsibility of a single unit. While epidemiologists are often regarded as informatics leads in LHDs, our assessment and exploration of the local workforce in Texas reveals a wider range of staff and programs becoming involved in day-to-day informatics-related practices. As more diverse staff take on informatics work, it is important to modernize job classifications to better define roles and avoid skill gaps. The constraints emphasized by participating LHDs reaffirm what other LHDs across the U.S. have faced and the need to expand resources and training (beyond Epi staff or a single program). While the COVID-19 pandemic added unprecedented burden to the public health workforce as a whole, LHDs were specifically impacted by overwhelming data-related demands, pressuring already limited informatics resources and staff. Nonetheless, our findings underscore how informatics partnerships have served as assets and helped mitigate resource gaps. It is through collaboration and partnership development that many informatics-related efforts and initiatives have been maximized during and post-COVID.

Given the limited sample size in this study, we cannot generalize findings to all Texas LHDs. Most LHDs in our sample were large health departments (according to TACCHO size definitions), which typically have more robust infrastructure and resources compared to smaller or rural LHDs. Differences also exist between LHDs and state agencies; therefore, we cannot generalize findings to the Texas DSHS informatics workforce. A future workforce needs assessment comparing local- and state-level challenges could provide further insight. Additionally, the terms “informatics” and “public health informatics” are broad terms that encompass a wide range of competencies and activities. While we attempted to recruit staff with sufficient knowledge of these terms and their application, we did not formally assess participants' knowledge or expertise in public health informatics. We also categorized informatics activities very broadly and did not compare them by organization level (e.g., operational vs. strategic) or by competency category (e.g., principles & strategies vs. information systems). Future research would benefit from these considerations to better identify areas of improvement. Regarding our interview findings, we acknowledge the possibility of participation/non-response bias due to our sampling strategy, as well as interviewer/interviewee bias. While we discuss partnerships as a key theme in our findings, we do not formally assess the quantity or quality of informatics partnerships across participating departments. Given the contributions of partner organizations, high and low maturity levels may be a reflection of the quantity and quality of those partnerships vs. workforce capacity and skills alone. This is another consideration for future research.

Health departments have faced many challenges in the integration and management of informatics within their organizations. While state health departments have contributed their expertise locally, local health department (LHD) staff must be able to carry out a wide range of informatics activities without the assistance of the state (1). A capacity and needs assessment survey conducted in 2015 described LHDs' top informatics activities as the extraction of data from information systems (69.5%) and the use and interpretation of quantitative (66.4%) and qualitative (55.1%) data while using geographic information systems (45.0%) or other analytical software (39.7%) (1). Unfortunately, research has shown that most public health professionals may not possess the necessary skills to use information effectively or even be aware of the importance of informatics (2).
